title: Basis Overlap Architecture for Electron Density Prediction
one_liner: Graph neural networks predict electron density by passing messages through the overlap table of the basis functions atoms use to describe electrons.
lead: Predicting how electrons arrange inside molecules is a core task in drug discovery and materials science. However, quantum mechanical calculations that give exact answers are far too expensive for large molecules. This paper introduces BOA, a neural network trained to mimic those expensive calculations. The key idea: instead of learning arbitrary patterns, the network respects the mathematical structure of how electrons are actually described in quantum chemistry.

problem.h2: Why prediction matters, and why it is hard
paras: Drug discovery requires predicting how molecules will behave: where electrons will congregate, how much energy they hold, what reactions they can undergo. The gold standard is quantum mechanics, which solves a set of equations to compute an exact answer. But those calculations take hours or days per molecule.

A naive first attempt is to train a standard neural network to copy the answers: feed in the atom positions, output the electron density. This works on small molecules but breaks when you ask it to predict a larger molecule it has never seen. The network learned arbitrary shortcuts, not the underlying physics. It does not generalize.

callout.html: Instead of letting the network learn arbitrary patterns, the architecture bakes in the mathematical structure of quantum chemistry, so the network respects physics.

panels.title: 1. The quantum fact
panels.caption: In real chemistry, electrons sit in basis functions (mathematical foundations) that overlap with neighbors.

panels.title: 2. Naive neural network
panels.caption: Standard network learns arbitrary patterns, ignores basis overlap, fails on unseen sizes.

panels.title: 3. Graph neural network
panels.caption: Atoms as nodes, chemical bonds as edges. Messages flow between neighbors only.

panels.title: 4. Overlap matrix message passing
panels.viz_args: Atom A reads how its basis overlaps with neighbors, sends weighted messages, scales by that overlap.
panels.caption: Messages respect how basis functions physically overlap, not arbitrary weights.

panels.title: 5. Generalization
panels.caption: Same logic works for molecules two hundred atoms, trained only on nine-atom examples.

steps.text: Place each atom in 3D space as a node in a graph.
For each pair of nearby atoms, compute how much their basis functions overlap mathematically.
Each atom reads its local neighborhood and constructs messages weighted by overlap strength.
Atoms send and receive messages along bonds, aggregating information from neighbors.
After layers of message passing, each spatial point outputs a number representing electron density.

paras: The paper swaps the message passing rule inside a graph neural network. Instead of learning arbitrary message weights, it uses the actual overlap of basis functions (a table of numbers showing how much each pair of atoms' electron templates overlap).

hidden.h2: The overlap table: basis function connections
hidden.name: overlap strength between basis functions
paras: In quantum chemistry, electrons are described using basis functions: mathematical templates like Gaussians centered on atoms. Any two atoms in different positions have basis functions that overlap — the amount of overlap tells you how strongly electrons at one atom can influence electrons at the other.

BOA measures this overlap mathematically (a standard computation in quantum packages) and uses it to scale the neural network messages. High overlap means atoms message each other strongly; low overlap means weak messages. This grounds the network in real physics instead of arbitrary learned weights.

heat.caption: Darker means basis functions of those atoms overlap more strongly. Highlights show strong connections.

reads.html: The overlap table tells you which atoms' electrons talk to each other most directly, based on how their quantum templates align.
The overlap of basis functions is computed via standard quantum-chemistry linear algebra and used as edge weights in the message-passing scheme.

mechanism.h2: Why baking in physics makes it generalize
paras: The core problem with naive neural networks is they learn specific patterns for the training size range. A 9-atom molecule's electron density is learned as a table of specific tricks. When you feed in a 200-atom molecule, the network has never seen patterns on that scale and fails.

BOA avoids this trap by not learning message weights from scratch. Instead, the network learns how to transform messages using the overlap table as a scaffold. The overlap table is computed the same way for any size molecule — it is a mathematical property of quantum chemistry, not a learned parameter. So the network's logic scales: a large molecule still uses the same overlap-based message rule, just applied to more neighbors. The network learns the overall strategy once, then runs it on any size.

stages.s: Compute overlap table for basis functions
Build graph, each edge weighted by overlap
Electron density for each spatial point

math.words: Each atom updates its representation by summing scaled messages from neighbors, where the scale is the overlap between their basis functions.
math.equation: h_i^(l+1) = sigma( sum_j(l) O_ij * W * h_j^(l) )
symbols: updated representation of atom i after layer l
representation of neighboring atom j before layer l
overlap strength between atom i and j basis functions

worked.title: A concrete example with two atoms
lines: Atom A has representation h_A = [0.5, 0.3], Atom B has h_B = [0.2, 0.8].
Transform W applied: [0.5, 0.3] * W becomes [0.4, 0.5]; [0.2, 0.8] * W becomes [0.3, 0.6].
Scaled message from B to A: 0.6 * [0.3, 0.6] = [0.18, 0.36].
If overlap were low (0.1): message becomes [0.03, 0.06] — eighty percent weaker.
High-overlap neighbors dominate communication; low-overlap neighbors whisper. Physics steers the flow.

math.note: The overlap table ensures distant or weakly-coupled atoms exert less influence on each other, matching how electrons actually behave in molecules.

charts.title: Naive neural network
charts.note: Learns the training set but fails badly on anything different in size.

charts.title: BOA (this paper)
charts.note: Physics-grounded architecture generalizes across molecule sizes without retraining.

items.html: The overlap table assumes basis functions are known and centered exactly. If the quantum representation is nonstandard or incomplete, the overlap values become unreliable, and messages are based on false physics.
In deep graph networks, messages from distant atoms arrive at each node only after many layers. Very large molecules may need too many layers, and distant information gets diluted.

items.b: Only works for systems with basis functions.
items.html: The approach assumes the quantum system is described using basis functions (common but not universal). Other quantum representations may not have a natural overlap table.
BOA generalizes excellently to larger molecules from the same chemical family. Generalizing to entirely new element types or bonding patterns requires more caution.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small BOA network trained on 50 molecules up to 9 heavy atoms. Then predict electron density for a held-out molecule of 15 atoms. Compare the predicted density to the true quantum answer. Then test on a 50-atom molecule. The metric should show the network predicts the 50-atom case far more accurately than a naive network of the same size would.
demo.closing: The demo succeeds when BOA's gap is small and naive network's gap is huge. This proves that baking physics into the architecture allows the same learned rule to work on any molecule size, because the overlap rule is universal.
